1275.title: Gratitude, again
1275.hook: gratitude of heart, tongue and limbs
1275.howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, throughout the day, after meals, on waking and when asked how they are, and teachers describe gratitude as reaching the heart, the tongue and the deeds of the body.

segments.voice: Yesterday, patience, and your line: three patiences. Today, the station that walks beside it.

Cracked feet. That's the detail his wife Aisha remembers: the Prophet ﷺ would stand in prayer at night so long that his feet cracked. And she asks the obvious question. Why do this, when Allah has already forgiven you, past and future? If the reason for prayer were fear of punishment, he'd have no reason to stand. His answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, turns the whole thing over. Should I not be a grateful servant? He isn't standing to earn something. He's standing to thank someone.
screen: `FEET CRACKED FROM STANDING.` → `WHY, IF YOU'RE FORGIVEN?` → `SHOULD I NOT BE GRATEFUL?`

segments.voice: Gratitude in Arabic is shukr. Al-Ghazali, in the Revival, says it isn't one act but works through the whole person, and he names three places it lives. First, the heart: knowing where the gift came from. Not luck, not only your own effort, but Allah behind the hands that brought it. Second, the tongue: saying it out loud. Alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, is the plainest form. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's translation: "Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse." Talk about the good you've been given. Third, the limbs: using a gift the way the giver would love. Eyes used to see kindly. Hands used to help. Strength used to stand at night, as the Prophet did. In the Qur'an, the family of David is told to work in gratitude, so the work itself becomes the thanks. Al-Ghazali needs all three. Thanks in the heart alone stays private. Thanks on the tongue alone can be a reflex, a thank-you said without looking up. Thanks in the limbs alone can become a list of chores. Together it's one motion: I know it's a gift, I say so, and I use it well. And there's a promise, in Pickthall's words: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Patience held steady when it's hard. Gratitude is what the same heart does when it's good.
screen: `THE HEART: KNOW WHERE IT CAME FROM.` · `THE TONGUE: SAY IT ALOUD.` · `THE LIMBS: USE IT WELL.` · then, large: `IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing in your life right now: your hands, a person, the room you're in. First the heart, knowing it's a gift and not something you're owed; then the tongue, a quiet thank you, or alhamdulillah if you pray. Then the limbs: decide one way you'll use that very gift today, hands that help carry something, a voice that calls someone.
Gratitude. Shukr: thanks with the heart that knows the giver, the tongue that says so, and the limbs that use the gift well. Today's word.
Your line: thanks with all of me. Heart, tongue and hands, one motion. Rest well.

1276.title: Reliance after effort
1276.hook: trust after effort: the tied camel
1276.howItsDone: Muslims teach tawakkul as trust in Allah that follows real effort, and the saying 'tie your camel and trust' is a common way of reminding someone to do their part before leaving the result to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gratitude, and your line: thanks with all of me. Today, a man with a camel and an honest question.

Shall I tie it, or shall I trust? A man asks the Prophet ﷺ about his camel, and it sounds almost like a riddle. Should he tie up his camel and rely on Allah, or leave it loose and rely on Allah? If you truly trust, why bother with a rope? And if you bother with a rope, are you really trusting? The answer, recorded in the collection of al-Tirmidhi, is short. Tie it, and trust. Today, the station that lives in that and.
screen: `A MAN, A CAMEL, A QUESTION.` → `ROPE, OR TRUST?` → `TIE IT, AND TRUST.`

segments.voice: The station is tawakkul, reliance on Allah. The tied camel shows its shape: effort first, then trust, and neither cancels the other. The Qur'an puts the order plainly, speaking to the Prophet about consulting his companions, in Pickthall's translation: "And when thou art resolved, then put thy trust in Allah. Lo! Allah loveth those who put their trust (in Him)." Consult, think, decide, then trust. Another picture in al-Tirmidhi is easy to misread. The Prophet said that if people relied on Allah as He should be relied on, He would provide for them as He provides for the birds: they go out in the morning hungry and come back in the evening full. Some hear that as, sit still and food will come. But the birds go out. They fly all day. The trust is in the going out, not instead of it. So there are two ways to miss tawakkul. One is the loose camel: doing nothing and calling it faith. The other is quieter. You tie the camel, then tie it again, then sit up all night watching the knot. That's effort with no trust in it, and it's exhausting. Tawakkul is the step after the knot. You've done what a sensible person does. The result was never in your hands. So you hand it over, and you sleep. Gratitude used the gift well; reliance uses effort well, then lets go of what effort can't reach.
screen: `EFFORT, THEN TRUST.` · `RESOLVE, THEN RELY.` · `THE BIRDS GO OUT.` · `THE STEP AFTER THE KNOT.`

segments.voice: Bring up one thing you're worried about, a test, a payment, a conversation, someone's health, and ask the camel question: what's the one sensible rope within your reach, and when will you tie it? Then look at what's left over, the outcome, other people's choices, and let your hands open on your knees, as if setting that part down. If you pray, you can say hasbunallah, Allah is enough for us; if not, just breathe out and leave it there.
Reliance after effort. Tawakkul: doing what is yours to do, then trusting Allah with what was never in your hands. Today's word.
Your line: tie it, trust him. Tie the rope, then let the knot be. Until tomorrow.

1277.title: Contentment with decree
1277.howItsDone: Muslims describe rida as contentment with Allah's decree that still allows grief and tears, and some repeat the words 'I am pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as my way of life, and with Muhammad as messenger' in their morning and evening remembrance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reliance after effort, and your line: tie it, trust him. Today, being at peace with how it lands.

A son named Ibrahim is dying, and his father is the Prophet ﷺ. The father's eyes fill with tears. A companion is surprised to see it, and asks, in effect, you too, Messenger of Allah? His answer, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, holds two things at once. The eye weeps, and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And then, to his son: we are saddened by your parting. Tears, and grief, and no complaint against Allah, all in the same breath.
screen: `A FATHER BESIDE HIS SON.` → `THE EYE WEEPS.` → `ONLY WHAT PLEASES OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: The station is rida, being pleased, or content, with what Allah decrees. It sits right beside patience, and teachers of the path draw the difference carefully. Patience is holding steady when the taste is bitter. Rida goes a step further: the taste is still bitter, but the heart has stopped arguing with the One who served it. That's why the Prophet's tears matter so much. Rida is not a smile pasted over grief. He wept. He said he was saddened. What he didn't do was say anything against his Lord. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever is pleased with Allah as Lord, with Islam as a way of life, and with Muhammad as messenger has tasted the taste of faith. Notice the first thing on that list. Not pleased with every event; pleased with Allah, as Lord. And the Qur'an describes the pleasure going both ways, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah hath pleasure in them and they have pleasure in Him." Two more things rida is not. It isn't approving of wrong. Scholars distinguish accepting what Allah has decreed from accepting an injustice someone is doing, which you're still asked to stop if you can. And it isn't giving up effort; yesterday's camel still gets tied. You don't have to like the weather. You can stop shouting at the sky. And if grief ever feels like too much to carry, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `STILL BITTER, NO LONGER ARGUING.` · `THE EYE WEEPS, THE HEART GRIEVES.` · `PLEASED WITH ALLAH AS LORD.` · then, large: `THEY HAVE PLEASURE IN HIM.` · then: `NOT APPROVAL OF WRONG.`

segments.voice: Choose something small you've been quietly arguing with, the rain, a delay, a plan that changed; not an injustice, just a thing that is how it is. Notice the but it should have been different, and for one breath set the argument down; you're allowed to wish it were otherwise. If you pray, you can say radhitu billahi rabba, I am pleased with Allah as Lord; if not, simply say inside: this is how it is today.
Rida. Contentment: being pleased with Allah as Lord, so that even through tears the heart stops arguing with what He has decreed. Today's word.
Your line: pleased with him. Tears allowed, and no argument with the sky. See you tomorrow.

1278.title: Love of Allah
1278.hook: say, if you love Allah, follow me, and Allah will love you (3:31)
1278.howItsDone: Muslims speak of love of Allah as shown by following the Prophet's example and drawing near through required and voluntary worship, and teachers of the inward path describe it as one of the stations of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rida, contentment, and your line: pleased with him. Today, the station of love.

"If ye love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins." That's the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, telling the Prophet ﷺ what to say. Read it slowly; it's built in three moves. A condition: if you love. An action: follow me. And something coming back the other way: Allah will love you. Love isn't left as a feeling you announce. It's tested by what you do next.
screen: `IF YE LOVE ALLAH.` → `FOLLOW ME.` → `ALLAH WILL LOVE YOU.`

segments.voice: The word is mahabbah, love. It isn't only a word for poets. It's in the Qur'an, and it runs both ways. In Pickthall's translation of another verse, Allah will bring "a people whom He loveth and who love Him." He loves first in that line. So how does a person grow in it? The opening verse says: follow. Love shows up as imitation; people who love someone pick up their habits, their words, the way they treat others. Then there's a hadith qudsi, words the Prophet reported from Allah, in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it lays out the path step by step. My servant draws near to Me with nothing dearer to Me than what I have made obligatory. And My servant keeps drawing near with extra deeds until I love him. And when I love him, I become the hearing he hears with, the sight he sees with, the hand he holds with, the foot he walks with. Commentators are careful here. They warn against reading it as Allah becoming a person's body, and read it as a life so guided that the person hears, sees and acts as Allah would love. The order matters: the duties, then the extra, then the love, then a whole life changed by it. Love here doesn't start as a feeling you chase. It follows the steps, and then it changes the one who walks them.
screen: `LOVE RUNS BOTH WAYS.` · `LOVE SHOWS UP AS FOLLOWING.` · `DUTIES, THEN EXTRA, THEN LOVE.` · `THE HEARING HE HEARS WITH.`

segments.voice: Think of the extra deeds in the hadith, the ones nobody asks for: a short prayer beyond the required ones, a kind word to someone who can't return it, picking up litter on a street that isn't yours, feeding a bird. Choose one you could do, and let the reason be simple: not for thanks, not to feel good about yourself, just for love of the One it's for. If you pray, hold the verse, if ye love Allah, follow me; if not, hold the plain thought: this is for love.
Mahabbah. Love: Allah's love for His servants and theirs for Him, shown by following and drawing near. Today's word.
Your line: love follows. Duties, then extra, then love. I'll be here tomorrow.

1279.title: Fear and hope
1279.hook: the believer flies with two wings, fear and hope
1279.howItsDone: Muslim teachers describe fear of Allah and hope in His mercy as two things a believer holds together, and some families at a deathbed speak of Allah's mercy so that hope is strong at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahabbah, love of Allah, and your line: love follows. Today, love gets two wings.

A bird with one wing doesn't fly. It goes in circles on the ground. Ibn al-Qayyim, a later scholar who wrote about the stations of the path, used a bird to picture the heart on its way to Allah. Love, yesterday's station, is the head. And the two wings are fear and hope. Readers draw out the lesson: lose the wing of fear, and the bird tips into carelessness. Lose the wing of hope, and it tips into despair. Either way, it doesn't get off the ground.
screen: `ONE WING GOES IN CIRCLES.` → `LOVE IS THE HEAD.` → `FEAR AND HOPE ARE THE WINGS.`

segments.voice: In Arabic the pair is khawf and raja, fear and hope, and the Qur'an puts them side by side. Describing the believers at night, it says, in Pickthall's translation, that they "forsake their beds to cry unto their Lord in fear and hope." Not fear, then hope. Both, in the same prayer. Fear here isn't panic. It's taking seriously that your choices matter and a reckoning is real, the evening ledger from a few days ago. It keeps a person honest. Hope is trusting that Allah's mercy is bigger than your mistakes. In Pickthall's words: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." Hope keeps a person from giving up. Now the scene that holds both. In the collection of al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ visits a young man who is dying, and asks how he finds himself. The young man answers: I hope in Allah, and I fear my sins. The Prophet says that whenever these two come together in a servant's heart at a moment like that, Allah gives him what he hopes for and keeps him safe from what he fears. He didn't tell the young man to drop either one. He blessed the pair. So the question isn't fear or hope. It's whether both wings are still moving. And if hope ever feels gone, the dark kind that won't lift, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `KHAWF AND RAJA, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `FEAR KEEPS YOU HONEST.` · `HOPE KEEPS YOU GOING.` · `A YOUNG MAN, HOLDING BOTH.`

segments.voice: Bring up one thing you're worried about in yourself, a habit, a temper, something you keep putting off, and let it be the wing of fear: honest, not frantic. Then find the other wing, one real reason for hope about that same thing, a time you did better, someone who forgave you, and breathe as if both wings were moving together. If you pray, rest on the line: despair not of the mercy of Allah.
Fear and hope. Khawf and raja: taking your choices seriously, and trusting that mercy is bigger than your mistakes, held together like two wings. Today's word.
Your line: two wings. Neither one can fly alone; the bird needs both of them. Until tomorrow.

1280.title: Sincerity of intention
1280.hook: actions are by intentions (Bukhari), recalled from day 97
1280.tomorrow: The heart as a lump of flesh
1280.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to make their intention, niyyah, before acts of worship, and teachers of the inward path ask people to keep checking that their good deeds are done for Allah rather than for praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fear and hope, and your line: two wings. Today, the last of the stations, and the one underneath all the others.

Two travelers pack the same bags, take the same road, and arrive at the same city on the same day. From the outside, nothing tells them apart. We met their story long ago, on day ninety-seven: the hadith that opens Sahih al-Bukhari. Actions are by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. One of them left home for Allah and His Messenger. The other left for something in this world, some worldly gain or a marriage. The same move, and two completely different journeys.
screen: `SAME BAGS, SAME ROAD.` → `ACTIONS ARE BY INTENTIONS.` → `TWO DIFFERENT JOURNEYS.`

segments.voice: The word is ikhlas, sincerity: making something pure, clearing out whatever doesn't belong. The Qur'an uses the idea for religion itself. In Pickthall's translation, people are commanded to serve Allah, "keeping religion pure for Him." And the short surah that declares Allah's oneness, say, He is Allah, the One, carries the name al-Ikhlas. Pure oneness in belief, pure intention in action. A hadith in Sahih Muslim shows why teachers of the path take it seriously. It describes people brought for judgment who did impressive things. One fought and died in battle. One learned and taught and recited the Qur'an. One gave generously. Each is asked what he did, and each answers well. And each is told, in effect: you did it so that people would say you were brave, or learned, or generous, and it was said. The hadith ends hard for all three. But it isn't meant to make anyone afraid to do good. It's meant to make them check the label on the box. Ikhlas doesn't mean waiting for perfectly pure motives before you act. It means noticing, again and again, who the deed is for, and turning it back toward Allah. Think back across this part: repentance, watchfulness, the evening ledger, detachment, patience, gratitude, reliance, contentment, love, fear and hope. Every one of them can be done for show. Ikhlas is what keeps them real.
screen: `MAKING SOMETHING PURE.` · `AL-IKHLAS: PURE ONENESS.` · `SO IT WOULD BE SAID. AND IT WAS.` · `CHECK WHO THE DEED IS FOR.`

segments.voice: Choose one good thing you plan to do soon, a post, a donation, a favor, a prayer, a hard day's work, and ask quietly: who is this for? Let the honest answer come even if it's mixed, a bit for Allah, a bit for how it looks, and don't throw the deed away; just turn it, the way you'd turn a picture to face the right wall. If you pray, say inside, this is for You; if you don't, say, this is for the good of it, not for the credit.
Ikhlas. Sincerity: clearing a deed of everything but the One it's for, and checking, again and again, who you're really doing it for. Today's word.
Your line: intention is everything. Same bags, same road, and a different journey inside. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1280 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HEART AS A LUMP OF FLESH.`

1281.title: The heart as a lump of flesh
1281.word: The heart as a lump of flesh
1281.hook: there is a lump of flesh in the body: if it is sound, all is sound. it is the heart (Bukhari)
1281.howItsDone: Muslims learn this hadith as a teaching that the heart, the inner center of a person, governs everything else, and teachers of the inward path speak of keeping the heart sound and treating its diseases.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ikhlas, sincerity, and your line: intention is everything. Today, a new part of the path begins.

Put a hand flat on the left side of your chest. Under it, a muscle is doing its work without being asked. The Prophet ﷺ pointed at something like it in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, narrated by al-Nu'man ibn Bashir. Truly, in the body there is a lump of flesh. If it is sound, the whole body is sound. If it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Truly, it is the heart. One small piece of the body, and everything else follows it.
screen: `A HAND ON YOUR CHEST.` → `A LUMP OF FLESH.` → `TRULY, IT IS THE HEART.`

segments.voice: The heart in Arabic is qalb, and in the hadith it's called a mudghah, a small piece of flesh. That's the surprise: the thing everything depends on is small, plain and easy to overlook. Muslim teachers read it as pointing through the organ that pumps blood to the inner center of a person, the place where intentions are made. Yesterday's ikhlas lives there, and so does every station from these two weeks. Another hadith, in Sahih Muslim, says Allah does not look at your bodies or your appearance, but looks at your hearts and your deeds. And the Qur'an names what will help on the last day. In Pickthall's translation, it is the day when wealth and sons avail not, "Save him who bringeth unto Allah a whole heart." A whole heart, a sound one, qalb salim. That word sound is the hinge. Hearts can be healthy, and hearts can get sick. This new part of the path takes the sicknesses one at a time, arrogance, envy and others, the way a doctor would. First, look back at this week: gratitude with the whole self, the tied camel, contentment even through tears, love that follows, fear and hope as two wings, sincerity. All of it was heart-work. And the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have asked Allah, the Turner of hearts, to make his heart firm. Even he asked for his heart to be kept.
screen: `QALB: A SMALL PIECE OF FLESH.` · `ALLAH LOOKS AT YOUR HEARTS.` · `A WHOLE HEART: QALB SALIM.` · `HEARTS CAN GET SICK.`

segments.voice: Rest your palm flat on your chest and feel the beat, steady, asking nothing from you: this small thing is keeping you alive right now. Then ask gently how the other heart is today, the one the hadith points through, and name it in one word, heavy, light, busy, tight, calm, with no fixing. If you pray, recall the Prophet's words, O Turner of hearts; if not, keep your hand where it is and breathe.
The heart as a lump of flesh. The qalb: a small piece of the body that everything follows; when it is sound, all of you is sound. Today's word.
screen: `THE HEART AS A LUMP OF FLESH — today's word`.
